title: Doctor directory with JPA
scenario: Hand-written SQL for every doctor search; adding a 'speciality' filter took a week.
stack: Spring Boot 4.1.1 · Java 25 · Spring Data JPA · Hibernate 7 · @Entity, JpaRepository, derived queries, @EntityGraph · DTO records · PostgreSQL 17 · Flyway · Testcontainers
simulation: Doctors, clinics, phone numbers, salaries and notes are fictional demo data. The private columns exist so the trap test can show what leaks.

tabs.html:
Belongs in this tab

  • The real-life problem as a 3-step story
  • What we are building, and an everyday analogy
  • How it works in 4 steps
  • One question to check yourself
  • What this station is not
  • Key terms

Level 1, about 5 minutes. Plain language: no code.

The problem in real life

  1. A week per filter

    Every doctor search was SQL written by hand. Adding "speciality" meant new SQL, new mapping, new tests: a week.

  2. JPA, returned as is

    The team switched to JPA and returned the Doctor entity straight from the controller. Some requests failed with a lazy-loading error. The others sent each doctor's personal phone, salary and HR notes to every visitor of the public directory.

  3. The fix

    Entities stay inside the service. The API returns a small record with only what the directory shows, built while the database session is open.

The API's shape is a decision. Never let it be whatever the table happens to hold.

What are we building?

GET /doctors?speciality=…&city=… searches the public directory, and GET /doctors/{id} shows one doctor: name, speciality, city, registration number and clinic.

An everyday analogy

A hospital's notice board shows each doctor's name, speciality and room. The HR file with salary and home phone stays in the office. You copy what the board needs onto the board; you do not pin up the file.

How it works in 4 steps

  1. Pick a repository method for the filters given; Spring Data has written its query.
  2. Load doctors and their clinics in one query.
  3. Copy each into a DoctorView, inside the transaction.
  4. Return the views; the entities never reach the JSON writer.
Check yourself: if the entity has a @JsonIgnore on salary, is returning it fine?

Safer, but fragile: the next private column added to the table is public until someone remembers to hide it, and the lazy clinic can still fail. A DTO lists what is public; everything else is private by default.

What this station is not

  • Read-only. No adding or editing doctors here.
  • No appointments. Just the directory.
  • No full-text search. Exact speciality and city, any letter case.

Key terms

TermSimple meaningEveryday exampleIn this project
JPAA standard way to map Java classes to tables, so you work with objects instead of SQL rows.A translator between your language and the database's.jakarta.persistence
EntityA class whose objects are rows of a table, managed by Hibernate.A file card that is also the record in the cabinet.Doctor
RepositoryAn interface; Spring Data writes the code behind it.Asking the librarian instead of searching the shelves.DoctorRepository
Derived queryA query written from a method's name."Find by speciality and city, ordered by name".findBySpecialityIgnoreCaseAndCity…
DTOA plain object shaped for the API, separate from the entity.The visiting card, not the HR file.DoctorView
Lazy loadingA linked object is fetched only when first touched, while the session is open.A file fetched from storage when you ask, if the archive is still open.Doctor.clinic

Belongs in this tab

  • 1. Business problem
  • 2. Acceptance criteria
  • 3. Requirements

Level 2. What a teammate hands you before you build.

Business problem

Mediqo (a fictional clinic chain) wrote SQL by hand for every doctor search; adding a speciality filter took a week.

Acceptance criteria

  1. Given speciality=cardiology&city=PUNE, then Dr Asha Mehta and Dr Fatima Ali, by name.
  2. Given only a speciality, only a city, or neither, then the matching doctors; a speciality nobody has, an empty list.
  3. Given doctor 1, then exactly id, name, speciality, city, registration number, clinic and clinic address; no personal phone, salary or notes anywhere.
  4. Given a search of all doctors, then one database query, not one more per clinic.
  5. Given an unknown doctor, 404; a filter with digits or over 40 characters, or a non-numeric id, 400.

Requirements

  • Entities never leave the service; the API returns DoctorView.
  • open-in-view is off: no database access while JSON is written.
  • Flyway owns the schema; Hibernate only validates it.
  • Rules stay database constraints too: unique registration number, valid clinic, positive salary.

Learning objectives

  • Map tables with @Entity, @Id and @ManyToOne.
  • Use JpaRepository and derived query methods.
  • Separate entities from DTOs, and say why.
  • Explain lazy loading, open-in-view, and N+1 queries.

tabs.label: Edge cases & trap
tabs.html:
Belongs in this tab

  • 6. Edge cases and failure cases
  • 7. The trap, shown failing with a test

Every edge case points at the test that proves it.

Edge cases

CaseWhat happensProved by
Both filters, mixed caseTwo doctors, by namebothFiltersInAnyCase
One filter; none; nobody matchesThe right doctors; all six; emptyoneFilterOrNone
One doctor; any listExactly the view's fields; no phone digits anywhereoneDoctorAsTheDirectoryShowsThem
Searching every doctor1 query (3 without the entity graph)aSearchLoadsDoctorsAndClinicsInOneQuery
Duplicate registration, unknown clinic, zero salary, written directlyRefused by named constraintsnamedConstraintsHoldWithoutJava
An import with a duplicateRolled backaFailedImportLeavesTheDirectoryAsItWas
Unknown doctor; bad filters or id404; 400DoctorContractTest

The trap

Plausible but wrong

Returning entities directly as JSON, leaking fields and lazy-loading errors.

The test writes a Doctor entity with the app's own JSON mapper (Jackson 3), as the old controller did. Outside a transaction (open-in-view off), the lazy clinic cannot be loaded: LazyInitializationException … no session. Inside one (what open-in-view on would do), the JSON contains personalPhone, salaryPaise, internalNotes, and Hibernate's own hibernateLazyInitializer. A probe while building found a third outcome. With package-private getters on Clinic, the proxy was written as {"hibernateLazyInitializer":{}} with no error at all. Entities usually have public getters, so this station uses them and shows the two common outcomes. While building, adding the personal phone to the view turned 2 tests red. Removing the entity graph from the full list turned 1 red: 3 queries instead of 1.

package com.mediqo.doctors;

import org.hibernate.LazyInitializationException;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.transaction.support.TransactionTemplate;
import tools.jackson.databind.json.JsonMapper;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

/**
 * The first test written for this station: what the old controller did, returning the Doctor entity as JSON, with
 * the app's own JSON mapper. Two outcomes, both bad, depending on whether a transaction is still open.
 */
class EntityAsJsonTrapTest extends ApiTest {

    @Autowired
    JsonMapper json;
    @Autowired
    TransactionTemplate transaction;
    @Autowired
    DoctorDirectory directory;

    @Test
    void outsideATransactionTheLazyClinicCannotBeLoaded() {
        Doctor doctor = doctors.findById(1L).orElseThrow();   // the clinic is a placeholder until touched
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> json.writeValueAsString(doctor))
                .hasRootCauseInstanceOf(LazyInitializationException.class)
                .hasMessageContaining("no session");
    }

    @Test
    void insideOneEveryPrivateColumnLeaks() {
        // What open-in-view=true would have done: the session stays open while the JSON is written.
        String body = transaction.execute(status -> json.writeValueAsString(doctors.findById(1L).orElseThrow()));
        assertThat(body).contains("\"personalPhone\":\"90000 10001\"", "\"salaryPaise\":45000000",
                "\"internalNotes\":\"On notice period until December\"", "hibernateLazyInitializer");
    }

    @Test
    void theViewHasOnlyWhatTheDirectoryShows() {
        String body = json.writeValueAsString(directory.one(1L).orElseThrow());
        assertThat(body).doesNotContain("personalPhone", "salary", "internalNotes", "hibernate")
                .contains("\"clinic\":\"Mediqo Koregaon Park\"");
    }
}

Troubleshooting

You seeCauseFix
LazyInitializationException: Could not initialize proxy … no sessionA lazy link was touched after the transaction ended.Map to a DTO inside the transaction, or load the link with @EntityGraph.

src/main/java/com/mediqo/doctors/DoctorController.java

Does
Validates the filters and returns views.
Why
It never sees an entity.
Without it
Returning Doctor: the trap.
package com.mediqo.doctors;

import jakarta.validation.constraints.Pattern;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.ProblemDetail;
import org.springframework.web.ErrorResponseException;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PathVariable;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestParam;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

import java.util.List;

@RestController
class DoctorController {

    private final DoctorDirectory directory;

    DoctorController(DoctorDirectory directory) {
        this.directory = directory;
    }

    /** Both filters optional, any letter case: /doctors?speciality=cardiology&city=Pune */
    @GetMapping("/doctors")
    List<DoctorView> search(@RequestParam(required = false) @Pattern(regexp = "[\\p{L} ]{2,40}", message = "letters and spaces, 2 to 40") String speciality,
                            @RequestParam(required = false) @Pattern(regexp = "[\\p{L} ]{2,40}", message = "letters and spaces, 2 to 40") String city) {
        return directory.search(speciality == null ? null : speciality.strip(), city == null ? null : city.strip());
    }

    @GetMapping("/doctors/{id}")
    DoctorView one(@PathVariable long id) {
        return directory.one(id).orElseThrow(() -> {
            ProblemDetail p = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "No doctor " + id + ".");
            p.setTitle("Doctor not found");
            return new ErrorResponseException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, p, null);
        });
    }
}

src/main/java/com/mediqo/doctors/DoctorDirectory.java

Does
Chooses the repository method and maps to DoctorView.
Why
@Transactional(readOnly = true): the mapping runs while the session is open.
Without it
Mapping in the controller after the session closed: lazy-loading errors.
package com.mediqo.doctors;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;

/** Picks the query for the filters given and maps entities to views inside the transaction. */
@Service
class DoctorDirectory {

    private final DoctorRepository doctors;

    DoctorDirectory(DoctorRepository doctors) {
        this.doctors = doctors;
    }

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    List<DoctorView> search(String speciality, String city) {
        List<Doctor> found;
        if (speciality != null && city != null) {
            found = doctors.findBySpecialityIgnoreCaseAndCityIgnoreCaseOrderByName(speciality, city);
        } else if (speciality != null) {
            found = doctors.findBySpecialityIgnoreCaseOrderByName(speciality);
        } else if (city != null) {
            found = doctors.findByCityIgnoreCaseOrderByName(city);
        } else {
            found = doctors.findAllByOrderByName();
        }
        return found.stream().map(DoctorView::of).toList();
    }

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    Optional<DoctorView> one(long id) {
        return doctors.findWithClinicById(id).map(DoctorView::of);
    }
}

src/main/java/com/mediqo/doctors/DoctorRepository.java

Does
Derived query methods, each with an entity graph.
Why
A new filter is a new method name; @EntityGraph joins the clinic so there is one query.
Without it
One query for doctors plus one per clinic (N+1).
  • IgnoreCase becomes upper(…) = upper(…) in SQL.
  • findWithClinicById: words between find and By are free text, so the method can be named for what it does.
package com.mediqo.doctors;

import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.EntityGraph;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;

/**
 * Spring Data writes the queries from the method names: findBy + Speciality + IgnoreCase + And + City ... OrderBy Name.
 * Adding a filter is a new method name, not a week of SQL. @EntityGraph loads each doctor's clinic in the same query
 * (a join), so mapping to DoctorView does not run one more query per doctor.
 */
interface DoctorRepository extends JpaRepository<Doctor, Long> {

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "clinic")
    List<Doctor> findBySpecialityIgnoreCaseAndCityIgnoreCaseOrderByName(String speciality, String city);

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "clinic")
    List<Doctor> findBySpecialityIgnoreCaseOrderByName(String speciality);

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "clinic")
    List<Doctor> findByCityIgnoreCaseOrderByName(String city);

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "clinic")
    List<Doctor> findAllByOrderByName();

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "clinic")
    Optional<Doctor> findWithClinicById(Long id);
}

src/main/java/com/mediqo/doctors/DoctorView.java

Does
What the directory shows.
Why
Fields are listed on purpose; new private columns stay private.
Without it
Every column of the table in the public API.
package com.mediqo.doctors;

/** What the public directory shows. Personal phone, salary and notes are not here, so they cannot leak. */
record DoctorView(long id, String name, String speciality, String city, String registrationNumber, String clinic, String clinicAddress) {

    static DoctorView of(Doctor d) {
        return new DoctorView(d.getId(), d.getName(), d.getSpeciality(), d.getCity(), d.getRegistrationNumber(),
                d.getClinic().getName(), d.getClinic().getAddress());
    }
}

src/main/java/com/mediqo/doctors/Doctor.java

Does
The doctors table as an entity, with a lazy link to the clinic.
Why
Hibernate tracks and loads it; protected no-argument constructor for JPA.
Without it
Nothing to map rows to.
package com.mediqo.doctors;

import jakarta.persistence.Entity;
import jakarta.persistence.FetchType;
import jakarta.persistence.Id;
import jakarta.persistence.JoinColumn;
import jakarta.persistence.ManyToOne;
import jakarta.persistence.Table;

/**
 * A row of the doctors table, as Hibernate manages it. It holds private columns (personal phone, salary, notes) and a
 * lazy link to the clinic, which is why it never leaves the service: the API returns DoctorView instead.
 */
@Entity
@Table(name = "doctors")
public class Doctor {

    @Id
    private Long id;
    private String name;
    private String speciality;
    private String city;
    private String registrationNumber;
    private String personalPhone;
    private long salaryPaise;
    private String internalNotes;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "clinic_id")
    private Clinic clinic;

    protected Doctor() {   // for JPA
    }

    public Long getId() {
        return id;
    }

    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }

    public String getSpeciality() {
        return speciality;
    }

    public String getCity() {
        return city;
    }

    public String getRegistrationNumber() {
        return registrationNumber;
    }

    public String getPersonalPhone() {
        return personalPhone;
    }

    public long getSalaryPaise() {
        return salaryPaise;
    }

    public String getInternalNotes() {
        return internalNotes;
    }

    public Clinic getClinic() {
        return clinic;
    }
}

src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__clinics_and_doctors.sql

Both tables, named constraints, and an index for the search.

CREATE TABLE clinics (
    id      BIGINT       PRIMARY KEY,
    name    VARCHAR(80)  NOT NULL,
    city    VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,
    address VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE doctors (
    id                  BIGINT       PRIMARY KEY,
    name                VARCHAR(80)  NOT NULL,
    speciality          VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,
    city                VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,
    registration_number VARCHAR(20)  NOT NULL,   -- public: printed on prescriptions
    personal_phone      VARCHAR(15)  NOT NULL,   -- private: for the clinic only
    salary_paise        BIGINT       NOT NULL,   -- private
    internal_notes      VARCHAR(500),            -- private
    clinic_id           BIGINT       NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT doctors_registration_unique UNIQUE (registration_number),
    CONSTRAINT doctors_clinic_fk           FOREIGN KEY (clinic_id) REFERENCES clinics (id),
    CONSTRAINT doctors_salary_positive     CHECK (salary_paise > 0)
);
-- upper(), because Spring Data writes IgnoreCase as upper(column) = upper(?): an index on lower() would never be used.
CREATE INDEX doctors_speciality_city ON doctors (upper(speciality), upper(city));

src/main/resources/application.yaml

open-in-view: false and ddl-auto: validate, with why.

spring:
  application:
    name: mediqo-doctors
  mvc:
    problemdetails:
      enabled: true
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/mediqo
    username: mediqo
    password: mediqo
  jpa:
    # No database work after the service returns: a lazy association touched while writing JSON fails loudly
    # instead of quietly running extra queries during the response.
    open-in-view: false
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate   # Flyway owns the schema; Hibernate only checks the entities match it

package com.mediqo.doctors;

import org.hibernate.LazyInitializationException;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.transaction.support.TransactionTemplate;
import tools.jackson.databind.json.JsonMapper;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

/**
 * The first test written for this station: what the old controller did, returning the Doctor entity as JSON, with
 * the app's own JSON mapper. Two outcomes, both bad, depending on whether a transaction is still open.
 */
class EntityAsJsonTrapTest extends ApiTest {

    @Autowired
    JsonMapper json;
    @Autowired
    TransactionTemplate transaction;
    @Autowired
    DoctorDirectory directory;

    @Test
    void outsideATransactionTheLazyClinicCannotBeLoaded() {
        Doctor doctor = doctors.findById(1L).orElseThrow();   // the clinic is a placeholder until touched
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> json.writeValueAsString(doctor))
                .hasRootCauseInstanceOf(LazyInitializationException.class)
                .hasMessageContaining("no session");
    }

    @Test
    void insideOneEveryPrivateColumnLeaks() {
        // What open-in-view=true would have done: the session stays open while the JSON is written.
        String body = transaction.execute(status -> json.writeValueAsString(doctors.findById(1L).orElseThrow()));
        assertThat(body).contains("\"personalPhone\":\"90000 10001\"", "\"salaryPaise\":45000000",
                "\"internalNotes\":\"On notice period until December\"", "hibernateLazyInitializer");
    }

    @Test
    void theViewHasOnlyWhatTheDirectoryShows() {
        String body = json.writeValueAsString(directory.one(1L).orElseThrow());
        assertThat(body).doesNotContain("personalPhone", "salary", "internalNotes", "hibernate")
                .contains("\"clinic\":\"Mediqo Koregaon Park\"");
    }
}

Named constraints, a rollback, and the query count from Hibernate's statistics.

package com.mediqo.doctors;

import jakarta.persistence.EntityManagerFactory;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.stat.Statistics;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.transaction.support.TransactionTemplate;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

/** The table's rules with Java bypassed, a rollback, and how many queries a search costs. */
class DoctorDatabaseTest extends ApiTest {

    @Autowired
    TransactionTemplate transaction;
    @Autowired
    EntityManagerFactory entityManagerFactory;
    @Autowired
    DoctorDirectory directory;

    void insert(long id, String registration, long salary, long clinic) {
        jdbc.sql("INSERT INTO doctors (id, name, speciality, city, registration_number, personal_phone, salary_paise, clinic_id) VALUES (?, 'Dr Test', 'Neurology', 'Pune', ?, '0', ?, ?)")
                .params(id, registration, salary, clinic).update();
    }

    @Test
    void namedConstraintsHoldWithoutJava() {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> insert(100, "MMC-2011-04512", 1, 1)).hasMessageContaining("doctors_registration_unique");
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> insert(100, "MMC-2099-00001", 1, 9)).hasMessageContaining("doctors_clinic_fk");
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> insert(100, "MMC-2099-00001", 0, 1)).hasMessageContaining("doctors_salary_positive");
    }

    @Test
    void aFailedImportLeavesTheDirectoryAsItWas() {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> transaction.executeWithoutResult(status -> {
            insert(100, "MMC-2099-00001", 1, 1);
            insert(101, "MMC-2099-00001", 1, 1);   // same registration: the whole import rolls back
        })).hasMessageContaining("doctors_registration_unique");
        assertThat(doctors.count()).isEqualTo(6);
    }

    @Test
    void aSearchLoadsDoctorsAndClinicsInOneQuery() {
        Statistics stats = entityManagerFactory.unwrap(SessionFactory.class).getStatistics();
        stats.clear();
        directory.search(null, null);
        assertThat(stats.getPrepareStatementCount()).isEqualTo(1);   // @EntityGraph: a join, not 1 + one per clinic

        stats.clear();
        transaction.executeWithoutResult(status -> doctors.findAll().forEach(d -> d.getClinic().getName()));
        assertThat(stats.getPrepareStatementCount()).isEqualTo(3);   // without it: 1 for doctors + 1 per clinic (2)
    }
}

package com.mediqo.doctors;

import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.EntityGraph;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.Query;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;

/**
 * Spring Data writes the queries from the method names: findBy + Speciality + IgnoreCase + And + City ... OrderBy Name.
 * Adding a filter is a new method name, not a week of SQL. @EntityGraph loads each doctor's clinic in the same query
 * (a join), so mapping to DoctorView does not run one more query per doctor.
 */
interface DoctorRepository extends JpaRepository<Doctor, Long> {

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "clinic")
    List<Doctor> findBySpecialityIgnoreCaseAndCityIgnoreCaseOrderByName(String speciality, String city);

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "clinic")
    List<Doctor> findBySpecialityIgnoreCaseOrderByName(String speciality);

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "clinic")
    List<Doctor> findByCityIgnoreCaseOrderByName(String city);

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "clinic")
    List<Doctor> findAllByOrderByName();

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "clinic")
    Optional<Doctor> findWithClinicById(Long id);

    /** Follows doctor.clinic.id; the clinic is loaded by the same query. */
    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "clinic")
    List<Doctor> findByClinicIdOrderByName(Long clinicId);

    /** A projection: Spring Data fills this interface from the query's aliases. */
    interface SpecialityCount {
        String getSpeciality();

        long getDoctors();
    }

    @Query("select d.speciality as speciality, count(d) as doctors from Doctor d group by d.speciality order by count(d) desc, d.speciality")
    List<SpecialityCount> countBySpeciality();
}

package com.mediqo.doctors;

import jakarta.validation.constraints.Pattern;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.ProblemDetail;
import org.springframework.web.ErrorResponseException;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PathVariable;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestParam;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

import java.util.List;

@RestController
class DoctorController {

    record SpecialityCount(String speciality, long doctors) {
    }

    private final DoctorDirectory directory;
    private final DoctorRepository doctors;
    private final ClinicRepository clinics;

    DoctorController(DoctorDirectory directory, DoctorRepository doctors, ClinicRepository clinics) {
        this.directory = directory;
        this.doctors = doctors;
        this.clinics = clinics;
    }

    @GetMapping("/clinics/{id}/doctors")
    List<DoctorView> clinicDoctors(@PathVariable long id) {
        if (!clinics.existsById(id)) {
            ProblemDetail p = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "No clinic " + id + ".");
            p.setTitle("Clinic not found");
            throw new ErrorResponseException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, p, null);
        }
        return doctors.findByClinicIdOrderByName(id).stream().map(DoctorView::of).toList();   // the graph loaded each clinic
    }

    @GetMapping("/specialities")
    List<SpecialityCount> specialities() {
        return doctors.countBySpeciality().stream().map(c -> new SpecialityCount(c.getSpeciality(), c.getDoctors())).toList();
    }

    /** Both filters optional, any letter case: /doctors?speciality=cardiology&city=Pune */
    @GetMapping("/doctors")
    List<DoctorView> search(@RequestParam(required = false) @Pattern(regexp = "[\\p{L} ]{2,40}", message = "letters and spaces, 2 to 40") String speciality,
                            @RequestParam(required = false) @Pattern(regexp = "[\\p{L} ]{2,40}", message = "letters and spaces, 2 to 40") String city) {
        return directory.search(speciality == null ? null : speciality.strip(), city == null ? null : city.strip());
    }

    @GetMapping("/doctors/{id}")
    DoctorView one(@PathVariable long id) {
        return directory.one(id).orElseThrow(() -> {
            ProblemDetail p = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "No doctor " + id + ".");
            p.setTitle("Doctor not found");
            return new ErrorResponseException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, p, null);
        });
    }
}

Challenge 3 · design on paper, no code

When method names stop scaling

Product wants filters for speciality, city, language spoken, gender, fee range and availability, in any combination. Derived methods would need 64 names. Compare JPA Specifications, Querydsl, Query by Example and a hand-written SQL builder with parameters. Which keeps queries type-safe, which keeps them readable, and which makes indexes easy to plan?

The learner decides the design here, before opening the Code tab.

Implementation approach

  1. Write the schema in Flyway; set Hibernate to validate it.
  2. Write the entities and the repository's derived methods.
  3. Write the trap test: the entity as JSON, in and out of a transaction.
  4. Write the view and the service that maps inside a transaction; count the queries.

Design alternatives and trade-offs

ApproachWhat it costsVerdict
Entities in the service, DTO records in the APIA small mapping per view.Chosen
Return entities, hide fields with @JsonIgnoreNew columns are public by default; lazy links still fail.Fragile
open-in-view: trueLazy links load during JSON writing: hidden queries, connections held for the whole response.Hides problems
FetchType.EAGER on the clinicEvery load of a doctor loads the clinic, wanted or not.Rarely right
Interface projections straight from the repositoryNo entity at all for read-only views.Good for reads (challenge 2)

Database design

TableKey and constraintsMapped as
clinicsPK id@Entity Clinic
doctorsPK id, doctors_registration_unique, doctors_clinic_fk, doctors_salary_positive; index on upper(speciality), upper(city)@Entity Doctor, @ManyToOne(fetch = LAZY) to Clinic

The index uses upper() because that is what the generated SQL compares (see Set up & code); an index on lower(), the first version, could never have been used. Hibernate maps registrationNumber to registration_number by Spring Boot's naming strategy. ddl-auto: validate stops the app at startup if they ever disagree.

CREATE TABLE clinics (
    id      BIGINT       PRIMARY KEY,
    name    VARCHAR(80)  NOT NULL,
    city    VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,
    address VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE doctors (
    id                  BIGINT       PRIMARY KEY,
    name                VARCHAR(80)  NOT NULL,
    speciality          VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,
    city                VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,
    registration_number VARCHAR(20)  NOT NULL,   -- public: printed on prescriptions
    personal_phone      VARCHAR(15)  NOT NULL,   -- private: for the clinic only
    salary_paise        BIGINT       NOT NULL,   -- private
    internal_notes      VARCHAR(500),            -- private
    clinic_id           BIGINT       NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT doctors_registration_unique UNIQUE (registration_number),
    CONSTRAINT doctors_clinic_fk           FOREIGN KEY (clinic_id) REFERENCES clinics (id),
    CONSTRAINT doctors_salary_positive     CHECK (salary_paise > 0)
);
-- upper(), because Spring Data writes IgnoreCase as upper(column) = upper(?): an index on lower() would never be used.
CREATE INDEX doctors_speciality_city ON doctors (upper(speciality), upper(city));

Belongs in this tab

  • 15. Real-world considerations

A Foundations station: the considerations to know, no runbook.

Data exposure
A leaked column is a data breach. Review API responses as carefully as SQL: what fields leave the server?
Query counts
N+1 queries are invisible in development and painful in production. Count queries in tests, as this station does, for pages that list things.
open-in-view
Spring Boot enables it by default and logs a warning at startup. Turning it off early is easy; turning it off late breaks code that relied on it.
Schema ownership
Flyway changes the schema; ddl-auto: validate only checks. Never let Hibernate create or update production tables.

tabs.html:
Belongs in this tab

  • 16. Interview takeaways
  • 17. Self-check rubric

Answers are hidden until opened, so the learner tries first.

Interview takeaways

Why not return JPA entities from a REST controller?

They expose every mapped column, including private ones, tie the API to the table, and can trigger lazy loading (extra queries or LazyInitializationException) while JSON is written. Return DTOs.

What is open-in-view, and why turn it off?

It keeps the persistence session open until the response is written, so lazy links load in the view layer. That hides N+1 queries and holds a connection for the whole request. Off makes problems visible.

What is the N+1 problem?

One query for a list, then one more per item to load a link. Fix it with a fetch join or an entity graph.

How do derived query methods work?

Spring Data parses the method name (findBy + properties + keywords like IgnoreCase, OrderBy) and generates the query at startup; a misspelt property fails startup.

Entity vs DTO?

An entity is a managed row: identity, lazy links, change tracking. A DTO is a plain value shaped for one use, such as an API response.

This Foundations station has no flawed version to review. Use this checklist on any JPA endpoint:

  • Does any controller return an @Entity?
  • Is open-in-view off, and does the mapping happen inside a transaction?
  • How many queries does the list endpoint run for 50 items?
  • Does Hibernate validate the schema, or change it?
